Section 1 · The opportunity

Law firms sell one product: hours.
That just stopped being enough.

AI now does in minutes what law firms bill by the hour. The firms that come out ahead won’t use AI to do the same work faster — they’ll turn their expertise into products: revenue that scales with software, not headcount.

01

research drafting diligence review judgment
The same matter, with AI
judgment hours AI removes from the bill

AI compresses the compressible. Judgment remains — and judgment is what software alone can’t fake.

02
Goodwin’s Opportunity

Legal services is a ~$1 trillion industry. Software represents only ~3% of industry spend.Global legal services: ≈ $950B–$1T (2024)

Legal software: ≈ $25–30B — roughly 3% of industry spend

That layer is growing rapidly. Record capital is flowing into legal softwareClio raised $900M at a $3B valuation in 2024 — the largest funding round in legal software history., and startups and incumbent firms alike are building the platform that connects the next generation of companies with their lawyers.

Someone will own that layer. It should be Goodwin.

Section 2 · The vehicle

Built as a company, not an initiative.

A law firm is built — correctly — to sell hours: its economics, its systems, and its incentives all require it. A product needs the opposite: speed, iteration, equity, patient capital. Forcing one inside the other .

The Answer — A Goodwin-owned technology companyThe TechCo — a standalone technology company: Goodwin holds the majority; employees hold equity. Its first product is already being built — but no product is the company. The company is the asset.
Why standalone beats building inside the partnership
Leading in legal tech takes the top tier of engineers — people who work startup hours because they own the outcome. A partnership can’t grant equity; a company can.
The firm’s systems move deliberately — and for a regulated partnership, they should. But the TechCo competes with venture-backed startups, and beating them means moving at their pace: hires closed in days, tools bought without procurement cycles, product shipped weekly. Standing alone is what makes that speed possible.
Contained liability and no partnership exposure — if the venture stumbles, it stumbles alone. And a cap table keeps every future option open: outside capital, a spin-out, or a sale — none of it touching the firm.
The TechCo outlasts any single product: the team, the AI infrastructure, the entity and approvals, the distribution muscle — ready to build the next product the moment it’s needed. Individual product bets can win or lose; the machine that makes them compounds either way.
Section 2 · The vehicle

A technology company can’t give legal advice.
But without advice inside, there’s no moat.

The TechCo’s edge isn’t software alone — it’s software with a real lawyer behind it. Pure legal tech ends where the hardest problems begin: at judgment.

Two challenges to overcome

1.The TechCo can’t give the advice itself: ethics rules bar any company that isn’t a law firm from practicing law.

2.Goodwin’s lawyers bill at rates a product can’t carry: quick, in‑product advice needs economics built for it.

The Answer — A new kind of Goodwin lawyer Platform Counsel. A new group inside Goodwin Procter LLP: off-track attorneys, dedicated to the TechCo’s products and embedded inside them — with economics built for the work the billable hour no longer fits.
Inside the firm

Goodwin attorneys. Privileged advice, engagement letters, partner supervision.

iAn automated conflicts check and a click-through, limited-scope engagement letter — advice begins there, never before. Attorney conversations are privileged and visibly separate in the product.
Dedicated to the products

TechCo products and nothing else — never the firm’s deal work. Matters arrive AI-prepared; any specialty, one bench.

iOne bench, every specialty the products need — venture, employment, IP, real estate. Each matter is a limited-scope engagement owned end-to-end by one attorney: AI prepares, the attorney answers. And deal work never comes here — that always stays with the practice groups.

Off-partner-track pay, AI first pass, sustainable hours — judgment priced in credits, not tenths of an hour.

Section 3 · The first product

Every year, tens of thousands of companies are born onto the venture track. Very few make it through.

~58,000Delaware corporations formed each year
→
a small fractionever raise an institutional round
→
fewer stillreach the exits the track exists for

Most of the odds are out of a founder’s hands — market, timing, luck. The legal foundation isn’t. It’s set in the company’s first days — usually with no lawyer in the room, and nothing keeping track of what gets decided.

Section 3 · The first product

Two types of founders.

Every venture-track founder starts in one of two places: most without real counsel on Day 1 — and a fortunate few with Goodwin, or a firm like it, from the start. Their problems differ. What they share is what’s missing.

Type 1 — the majority Founding without counsel.

First-time founders with no lawyer in their network — making the company’s most consequential decisions without counsel.

Type 2 — the fortunate few Goodwin from Day 1.

World-class counsel — but a legal life stuck in email and routine work with no good home.

The common denominator — Neither has a system: one place where the company’s legal life lives.
Given all of that — Product #1

Section 4 · The economics

What this buys beyond the P&L

Six returns the model doesn’t count — like the premium-work line, deliberately uncounted upside.

Startups and rivals are building the platform that sits between the next generation of companies and their lawyers. If Goodwin owns it, it feeds the firm. If someone else owns it, it’s aimed at the firm. This return is invisible in the model — it shows up as revenue the firm never notices it didn’t lose.
Building the TechCo teaches Goodwin what no vendor contract can: shipping AI-native software, turning firm expertise into product, seeing how AI-prepared work changes a matter — muscle that flows back into how the firm delivers. Watching from the sidelines is the risk; this is learning by doing.
Outward, a credible answer to “what does a legal career look like in the AI era?” — a recruiting edge for lawyers and engineers alike. Inward, new paths for the people Goodwin already has: legal engineering and product-counsel roles, Platform Counsel off the partner track. Firms that offer that future recruit better — and keep more.
A firm that builds and keeps a product company earns a different reputation with clients, recruits, and the legal-tech market. The position is hard to copy because it takes three things together: the firm’s expertise inside the products, its attorneys behind them, and a structure built to hold both.
Every product the TechCo ships is a window into how a market behaves — anonymized, consented data on terms, timing, and practice. Keel opens that window onto the startup market first; each future product opens another. All of it sharpens the advice the firm sells.
Productized expertise drops the price of legal support wherever the TechCo points it — founders first, other underserved markets as the products multiply. An access-to-law story that stands up with regulators, the press, law schools, and the firm’s own people.

02Counsel Credit menu

Counsel Credits: $245 single · 3-pack $650 (~12% off) · 6-pack $1,235 (~16% off) · 9-pack $1,765 (~20% off). Packs last 12 months. One currency for all attorney work beyond what subscriptions include. You always see the credit price in the product before you commit — no hourly billing, ever. Credit revenue is legal fees — it goes to Goodwin Procter LLP, never the TechCo. Blended realized ≈ $215/credit at an assumed launch mix. The ladder is deliberate: bulk buyers are the healthiest customers, and the discount deepens the habit.

Why Keel docs cost 1 and outside paper costs 3: Keel documents are faster to review (known templates, AI pre-checked) — and the discount rewards keeping your paperwork standardized in Keel, which keeps your whole record clean. Excluded at every level (referred to Goodwin or a specialist): litigation, M&A, IPOs, government investigations, patent/trademark filings, tax, immigration. SAFE rounds run entirely through the platform’s Rounds feature — the round’s documents are reviewed with credits (typically 2–4 per round); there is no separate SAFE package. Credit prices are launch prices to be validated: consumption is Keel’s price lever; subscriptions are its funnel and stay flat.

Fractional GC and Chief Counsel tiers, fund portfolio blocks, and the full cost-and-realization math live in the financial model — available upon request. Every price is a launch price, to be validated in beta.

Why the math works

Every price rests on one engine: the AI does everything except the judgment. By the time work reaches an attorney it’s been drafted, checked, and briefed from the company’s own record — so the attorney delivers judgment in 15–30 minutes, not hours.

The subscription is deliberately not where attorney work lives: $149/month covers the platform plus the relationship — a named attorney, a quarterly call, simple questions by message. Attorney work runs on credits: $245 each, $650 for three.

A credit is priced at roughly what an attorney-hour is worth. The customer pays $245 for work that costs $600+ elsewhere; the attorney realizes $490–735 per hour worked. Both sides win — and the spread funds the model: big-law realization at startup prices, AI doing the compression in between.

Why the subscription is priced where it is

Founders today resent paying for software. They compare every SaaS line item to what they could vibe-code themselves in a weekend, they cancel anything that smells like enterprise pricing, and they’re right about half the time. Price Keel the way legal-tech usually prices — hundreds a month, “contact sales” — and the founder’s reflex is I’ll build a doc generator and a deadlines spreadsheet myself. At $149, the reflex never fires: it’s less than an hour of any lawyer’s time, and no weekend project comes with a named attorney behind it. That’s the part they can’t build — so the price sits exactly where they never stop to ask the question.

The subscription isn’t where the model makes its money. Its job is to bring companies in at formation — before anyone competes for them — and make Keel their system of record: cap table, contracts, deadlines, institutional memory. Everything else monetizes that position. Customers already inside buy credits when work arrives. Companies that outgrow credits move up to fractional tiers. And when the first institutional round comes, an ECVC partner inherits a client no competitor has heard of. The price stays flat as the company grows, so success never gives a founder a reason to leave. The subscription buys the record; the record earns everything else.

How we win

Win the search founders already run. “how do I start a company” — the query that leads to LegalZoom today should land on Keel’s free formation. That means SEO — and increasingly, being the answer ChatGPT and the other AI assistants give when founders ask them.

Arrive first, become the record. Customers acquired at the moment of incorporation — before any competitor knows the company exists.

Distribution no startup can buy. Goodwin’s VC relationships, accelerator partnerships, and brand — channels legal-tech competitors spend years chasing.

The firm funnels Type 2 in. ECVC partners put their existing clients on the platform as part of how they work together — adoption built into the relationship, no sales motion required.

New business for ECVC. Every Type 1 company that reaches its first institutional round arrives at ECVC — deal work the firm otherwise wouldn’t have seen, from a pipeline it never had to originate.

Type 1 — founding without counsel

Who they are. The majority of new venture-track founders: first-timers, often technical, with almost no cash and no lawyer in their network. They’re incorporated and operating from week one — splitting equity with a co-founder, hiring a first contractor, signing a first customer — legal decisions, made immediately. Calling an Am Law 50 firm doesn’t even occur to them.

⌕  how do I start a company
So they Google it.
→
They incorporate with a formation site.
LegalZoom or the like — a filing, not counsel.
→
Then ChatGPT becomes their lawyer.
Generic answers, no context, no accountability — and the record lives nowhere.

The problem. The earliest decisions — entity, equity, governance, IP — are set in the company’s first days, exactly when counsel is least affordable. So the company’s most consequential decisions get made without counsel, on tools that don’t connect to a lawyer and don’t keep a record.

Type 2 — Goodwin from Day 1

Who they are. The fortunate few: funded or well-connected companies that have Goodwin — or a firm like it — from Day 1, with an ECVC deal team already behind them. The counsel is world-class; the experience around it hasn’t caught up.

Problem one — no single source of truth. The work product is excellent, but it lives in emails, attachments and closing sets. A simple factual question about their own company means emailing their lawyer and waiting. Founders live in software: they expect the answer to be on a dashboard — always on, always current.

Problem two — work that was never a lawyer’s job. Below the deal work sits a band of routine, administrative tasks that fit neither the billable hour nor a lawyer’s time — work ECVC and practices across the firm effectively lose money on today. That is exactly the work AI should now do.

The attorney relationship

Every paid subscription includes a named attorney — a Platform Counsel lawyer who knows the company’s record. AI does the first pass; the attorney brings the judgment. And once a company has raised its first institutional round, it also has a named ECVC partner leading the relationship. Which lawyer handles what depends on the work:

Deal & specialist workEvery institutional round, from term sheet on — plus M&A, litigation, and other specialist matters.
Served byECVC deal teams— and other practice groups as the matter requires
Routine, bounded mattersContracts, filings, quick questions — done by the software; when a lawyer’s judgment is needed, it’s priced in credits.
Served byPlatform Counsel

Platform Counsel works on credits — menu-priced, quoted in the product before any commitment. Activation is one automated conflicts check and a click-through, limited-scope engagement letter; once activated, the relationship includes the quarterly check-in calls plus anytime messaging for questions that need judgment — all privileged, all in the product.

What’s failed before — and what we learned

Two attempts came before us: a startup that added lawyers, and a law firm that added software. Each teaches one precise lesson.

Atrium (2017–2020) · the startup that added lawyers

Justin Kan raised ~$75.5M to run a software company and its own law firm as one business, selling legal services at flat subscription prices. The idea was that software would make the lawyers efficient enough to turn a profit at those prices. The software never delivered that efficiency — so every subscription was underpriced legal work done by expensive salaried lawyers, and growth only multiplied the loss. The attempted fix made it worse: Atrium pivoted to pushing legal work out to partner firms, clients no longer knew who their lawyer was, and they left. It shut down in March 2020 and returned capital.

The mistake: Atrium set prices that assumed efficiency its software didn’t yet deliver — and the pivot that followed destroyed the client relationship.

SixFifty (2019–2025) · the firm that added software

Wilson Sonsini did what we propose — built a software subsidiary. SixFifty automated employment and HR documents, and it worked. Then, in July 2025, the firm sold it. The question worth studying isn’t why it failed — it didn’t — but why the firm let it go: SixFifty was severable. A niche product, no WSGR lawyer inside it, no work flowing back to the firm — a good asset the partnership happened to own, worth more as cash than as strategy. And a partnership holds side assets badly: profits distribute annually, and a decade-long product bet keeps losing the annual argument. Baker McKenzie’s 2024 spin-out of SCORE fits the same pattern.

The lesson: a firm can build a software company. Keeping one takes a product the firm can’t afford to sell — and a structure built to hold it.

Why the TechCo is neither

1 · The money stays separate. Legal fees go to the lawyers; software revenue goes to the TechCo. Atrium lost money because one side quietly paid for the other — here, the two never touch.

2 · We built it before we priced it. Atrium promised savings its software hadn’t produced yet. Our product already exists — and attorney work is priced on the time the AI actually saves, not the time we hope it will.

3 · The customer always knows who their lawyer is. A named Goodwin attorney, an engagement letter, a conflicts check — every time. The confusion that drove Atrium’s clients away can’t happen.

4 · Selling the TechCo’s products would hurt Goodwin — selling SixFifty didn’t hurt Wilson Sonsini. SixFifty sent nothing back to its firm, so selling it cost nothing. The TechCo’s products send clients and deals to Goodwin — no one sells their own pipeline. And it lives in a company built to be kept: equity, its own capital, no annual budget fight.

Atrium had no firm behind it. SixFifty had no reason to stay. The TechCo has both — a firm behind it, and a product the firm can’t afford to sell.
